title: Testing IaC & Managing Drift
summary: Guarding infrastructure changes the way you'd guard application code — review, automated policy, and drift detection, not just hoping applies go well.

slides.markdown:
The standard gate: a pull request triggers CI to run `terraform plan` and post the output as a PR comment, so a human reviews the **actual diff** — not just the HCL change — before anyone runs `apply`. Merging (or a separate approval step) then triggers the real `apply`, using the exact plan that was reviewed, not a freshly recomputed one that might differ if something changed in the meantime.

This is the infrastructure equivalent of code review: the diff a reviewer approves should be the diff that actually gets executed, with no gap where drift could sneak in between review and apply.

Human review doesn't scale to catching every dangerous pattern every time — **policy-as-code** (Open Policy Agent/Rego, or HashiCorp Sentinel) runs automated rules against a plan before it's allowed to apply. A policy might say: "no security group may allow ingress from `0.0.0.0/0` on port 22" or "every S3 bucket must have encryption enabled" — checked mechanically, every single time, regardless of who's applying.

This moves guardrails from "a reviewer has to remember to check" to "the pipeline mechanically refuses," the same shift unit tests bring to application code.

A scheduled CI job runs `terraform plan` on a cadence (nightly, hourly) with **no apply** — a healthy environment should show "No changes." Any diff means something changed reality without going through the pipeline: a manual console tweak, an expired resource, an out-of-band script.

The value here is catching drift **before** a human notices something's subtly broken in production — a scheduled plan turning up a diff is a signal to investigate immediately, not a routine event to ignore.

IaC testing spans a spectrum from cheap-and-fast to slow-and-realistic.

| Approach | Speed | Catches |
|---|---|---|
| Static validation (`terraform validate`, `tflint`, policy-as-code) | Seconds | Syntax errors, style issues, policy violations |
| Plan-only review | Seconds–minutes | "Does this diff do what I expect" |
| Provisioning in a real sandbox | Minutes | Actual provider behavior, integration issues static checks can't see |

Static checks run on every commit; full sandbox provisioning is reserved for higher-risk changes or scheduled runs, since it costs real time and real cloud spend.

slides.subTitle: A policy blocking a dangerous plan
slides.markdown:
A simplified Rego-style policy check, conceptually:

```
deny[msg] {
  resource := plan.resource_changes[_]
  resource.type == "aws_security_group_rule"
  resource.change.after.cidr_blocks[_] == "0.0.0.0/0"
  resource.change.after.from_port <= 22
  resource.change.after.to_port   >= 22
  msg := "SSH open to the internet is not allowed"
}
```

This runs against every plan automatically, in CI, before any apply — the exact rule that stops a database security group opened to the world from ever reaching production, without a human having to catch it by eye.

slides.subTitle: Applying from an untracked laptop
slides.markdown:
**The wrong belief:** "I'll just run `terraform apply` from my laptop real quick, it's a small fix."

**Why it breaks:** a laptop apply bypasses every guardrail here — no PR review, no policy check — and can run against a **local, uncommitted** copy of code, silently diverging applied infrastructure from the repo. Nobody notices until an incident.

**The correct model:** every apply against shared infrastructure goes through the pipeline — even a one-line fix — so applied state and the repo never quietly disagree.

Guarding IaC the way you'd guard application code means four layers stacked together: **static validation** on every commit, **plan review** in a pull request, **policy-as-code** enforcing rules mechanically, and **scheduled drift detection** catching anything that slipped through outside the pipeline entirely.
